question: A hairy-footed hobbit named Bilbo finds a magic gold ring in a cave while playing a riddle game with a creature named Gollum. Who wrote the 1937 children's book?
context: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an Oxford philology professor. The Hobbit was published in September 1937 by Allen & Unwin in London. Tolkien's sequel grew into the three-volume Lord of the Rings (1954-55).

question: In Tolkien's Lord of the Rings, the young hobbit who inherits the One Ring from Bilbo and must carry it to be destroyed is named what?
context: Frodo is Bilbo's cousin (often called nephew). The Ring must be carried to Mount Doom in Mordor to be unmade. Tolkien wrote the first volume, The Fellowship of the Ring, in 1954, twelve years after he began work on it.

question: Tolkien's fire-breathing dragon who sleeps on a mountain of gold under the Lonely Mountain in The Hobbit is named what?
context: Smaug captured the Lonely Mountain (Erebor) and its dwarven gold-hoard centuries before The Hobbit begins. Tolkien drew Smaug himself for the book's illustrations. Benedict Cumberbatch voiced Smaug in Peter Jackson's 2013 film adaptation.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's most famous poem, published in 1845, features a black bird that lands on a bust above a chamber door and croaks a single repeated word. What word?
context: The Raven appeared in the New York Evening Mirror on January 29, 1845. It made Poe instantly famous but earned him only $9. The bust the raven perches on is of Pallas Athena. The narrator's lost love is named Lenore.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs created a famous jungle hero raised by apes in the African jungle after his parents Lord and Lady Greystoke die. What's the character's name?
context: Tarzan of the Apes debuted in All-Story Magazine in October 1912. His ape name Tarzan means White-Skin in the language of the great apes Burroughs invented. He inherits the title Lord Greystoke from his father.

question: A 1930s pulp magazine hero in a slouch hat and black cloak fights crime with twin .45 automatics, asking 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?' Who is he?
context: The Shadow debuted in Detective Story Hour radio in 1930 and as a pulp character in 1931 (written mostly by Walter Gibson under the pen name Maxwell Grant). The radio tagline finished: 'The Shadow knows!'

question: H.P. Lovecraft's most famous creature is a giant green octopus-headed dragon-winged horror that sleeps beneath the Pacific in a sunken city. What's it called?
context: Cthulhu debuted in The Call of Cthulhu in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales. The sunken city is called R'lyeh. Lovecraft admitted no human mouth could properly pronounce the name; he suggested 'Khlûl'-hloo.'

question: Robert E. Howard's most famous pulp character is a black-haired Cimmerian barbarian who eventually becomes king of Aquilonia. Who is he?
context: Conan first appeared in Weird Tales in December 1932 in the story 'The Phoenix on the Sword.' Howard wrote 21 Conan stories before his suicide in 1936. Arnold Schwarzenegger played him in the 1982 John Milius film Conan the Barbarian.

question: Raymond Chandler's hardboiled Los Angeles private detective, who debuted in 1939's The Big Sleep, is named what?
context: Marlowe appears in seven Chandler novels. Humphrey Bogart played him in the 1946 film of The Big Sleep. Chandler's other novels include Farewell My Lovely (1940), The Long Goodbye (1953), and The Lady in the Lake (1943).

question: Isaac Asimov's series about a Galactic Empire's fall and a mathematician's plan to shorten the dark age using statistical prediction is called what?
context: Asimov began the Foundation stories in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1942. The mathematician's name is Hari Seldon; his predictive science is called psychohistory. The original trilogy was published as books between 1951 and 1953.

question: Frank Herbert's 1965 sci-fi epic about a desert planet, giant sandworms, and a spice called melange that lets navigators fold space is called what?
context: Herbert based the desert ecology on his research on Oregon coastal dunes for an unfinished article. The book was rejected by 20 publishers before Chilton Books (a manuals publisher) bought it. Sandworms can be over 400 meters long.

question: Ray Bradbury's 1953 novel about a future fireman whose job is to burn books takes its title from the temperature at which paper ignites. What's the title?
context: Bradbury wrote the original novella in nine days on a rented typewriter in the basement of UCLA's Powell Library at ten cents per half-hour. The fireman protagonist is Guy Montag; his wife is Mildred. The title's temperature isn't quite accurate — paper actually ignites around 480°F.

question: In Tolkien's stories, the wise old wizard with a long gray beard and pointy hat who organizes Bilbo's quest and later leads Frodo's fellowship is named what?
context: Gandalf is called Mithrandir by the Elves and Tharkûn by the Dwarves. He is one of the Istari, sent to Middle-earth as a Maia (angelic being) in the shape of an old man. Ian McKellen played him in Peter Jackson's films.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 short story about a murderer driven mad by what he imagines is the steady beating of his victim's heart under the floorboards is called what?
context: First published in The Pioneer in January 1843. The unnamed narrator kills an old man with a 'vulture eye' and hides him under the floor, then confesses when he believes the police can hear the corpse's heart still beating.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Civil War veteran is transported to Mars (called Barsoom by its inhabitants), where he gains super-strength from the lower gravity and falls in love with Princess Dejah Thoris. What's his name?
context: A Princess of Mars debuted in All-Story Magazine in February 1912, six months before Tarzan. Carter is a Virginia gentleman. Burroughs wrote eleven Barsoom novels through 1948. The 2012 Disney film John Carter was a famous box-office bomb.

question: Tolkien's master enemy in The Lord of the Rings — the dark lord whose Eye watches from a tower in Mordor and who made the One Ring — is named what?
context: Sauron was originally a Maia (servant of the Valar) under Morgoth, the first Dark Lord. His tower is Barad-dûr. His Eye is fashioned in the Eye of Sauron iconography by Peter Jackson; in the books it is more metaphorical. The One Ring contains a fragment of his power.

question: Dashiell Hammett's 1930 detective novel features a black bird statuette sought by a circle of murderers and an unflappable San Francisco PI named Sam Spade. What's the bird?
context: The novel was serialized in Black Mask magazine in 1929-30 before publication. John Huston's 1941 film with Humphrey Bogart as Spade is considered a defining work of film noir. The bird turns out to be a lead fake — the prize was a hoax.

question: Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel about a bounty hunter who 'retires' lifelike androids was adapted into Ridley Scott's 1982 cyberpunk film. What was the film called?
choices: The Man in the High Castle
context: Dick's novel was Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? Scott's film starred Harrison Ford as Rick Deckard and Rutger Hauer as Roy Batty. Dick died in March 1982, three months before the film's release. The title 'Blade Runner' came from an unrelated William S. Burroughs / Alan Nourse work.

question: The 1937 Tolkien novel about a hobbit hired by thirteen dwarves to recover their stolen gold from a dragon under a mountain is titled what?
context: Full title: The Hobbit, or There and Back Again. The thirteen dwarves are led by Thorin Oakenshield. The first edition was 1500 copies and sold out by Christmas 1937. C.S. Lewis was one of the first reviewers and praised it warmly.

question: Mickey Spillane's hard-drinking, fast-shooting New York private eye who debuted in 1947's I, the Jury is named what?
context: Spillane wrote the first Hammer novel in 19 days. By 1980, seven of the top fifteen best-selling fiction titles of all time were Mike Hammer novels. Spillane himself starred as Hammer in the 1963 film The Girl Hunters.

question: Arthur C. Clarke's 1968 collaboration with Stanley Kubrick that gave us HAL 9000 and the mysterious black space-monolith is called what?
context: Clarke and Kubrick developed the novel and film concurrently. The book came out four months after the film's April 1968 release. The story expands Clarke's 1948 short story The Sentinel. HAL stands for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer.

question: Bram Stoker's 1897 horror novel about a Transylvanian count who relocates to England and preys on young women launched countless adaptations. Who is the count?
context: Stoker partly modeled Dracula on the 15th-century Wallachian prince Vlad III, Vlad the Impaler. The novel is epistolary — diary entries, letters, telegrams. Bela Lugosi's 1931 film performance defined the screen image of the vampire.

question: A 1933 pulp magazine and 181-novel series featured a bronze-skinned scientist-adventurer and his five-man team of specialists. The hero is called the Man of Bronze. What's his name?
context: Doc Savage (Clark Savage Jr.) debuted in March 1933. Lester Dent wrote most of the novels under the house pen name Kenneth Robeson. Doc's headquarters were on the 86th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper modeled on the Empire State Building.

question: Tolkien's One Ring must be cast into the fires of which mountain in Mordor where it was forged?
context: Mount Doom (Orodruin in Sindarin, Amon Amarth) is an active volcano in central Mordor. Sauron forged the Ring there in the Second Age. The Ring can be unmade only in the same fires that forged it. The mountain stands within sight of Sauron's tower Barad-dûr.

question: On June 11, 1936, in his small Texas home, Robert E. Howard learned his mother had fallen into her final coma and walked outside to his Chevrolet to take his own life at age 30. The town later became a pilgrimage site for pulp fans. What Texas town did Howard live in?
context: Howard's mother Hester died the next day, June 12, 1936. The Howard House Museum opened in Cross Plains in 1989. Howard had been correspondents with Lovecraft from 1930 until his death, exchanging letters that ran tens of thousands of words.

question: H.P. Lovecraft lived almost his entire life in a single American city, returning there from a brief disastrous marriage in New York. He wrote most of his stories in his attic study. What city was his lifelong home?
context: Lovecraft was born in Providence on August 20, 1890 and died there March 15, 1937 of intestinal cancer. He briefly lived in Brooklyn 1924-26 after marrying Sonia Greene; the experience deepened his xenophobia and informed The Horror at Red Hook. Many of his fictional towns (Arkham, Innsmouth, Kingsport) are based on real New England locations.

question: In March 1923, a Chicago-based fiction magazine launched that would become the home for Howard, Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and the founding voices of cosmic horror and sword and sorcery. The magazine ran until 1954 under multiple revivals. What was it called?
context: Weird Tales was founded by Jacob Henneberger. Farnsworth Wright edited it through its 1930s golden age. The signature triumvirate — Lovecraft, Howard, and Clark Ashton Smith — anchored the magazine in the early 1930s while corresponding with each other constantly.

question: Tolkien served as a signals officer at the Battle of the Somme in 1916, where many of his closest school friends from the T.C.B.S. club died. He later said his experiences in the trenches shaped a particular Hobbit character. Who?
context: Tolkien specifically named Sam as inspired by the working-class English privates who served under him. The T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society) had four members; two — Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Smith — died in 1916. Tolkien was invalided home with trench fever in November 1916 and survived.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 story about a Parisian amateur detective who solves the murders of two women in a locked apartment using pure deduction is widely considered the first modern detective story. What's the detective's name?
context: The Murders in the Rue Morgue (April 1841 in Graham's Magazine) introduced detective fiction's foundational conventions: the brilliant amateur sleuth, the slower narrator-companion, the locked-room mystery, the dramatic reveal. Conan Doyle named Poe's stories as the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes.

question: John W. Campbell took over an Astounding magazine in 1937 and launched what is now called the Golden Age of science fiction, publishing Asimov, Heinlein, Sturgeon, and van Vogt. One of his own 1938 novellas became the basis for John Carpenter's 1982 horror film. What was the novella?
context: Who Goes There? appeared in the August 1938 issue under Campbell's pen name Don A. Stuart. The story features Antarctic researchers and a shape-shifting alien. It was first adapted as The Thing from Another World (1951) and then Carpenter's The Thing (1982). Campbell edited Astounding (renamed Analog in 1960) until his death in 1971.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs published the first Tarzan story in October 1912 in the same New York pulp magazine that had published John Carter eight months earlier. Tarzan's parents are stranded by mutineers on the African coast and die before he can speak. What's their family title?
context: John Clayton, the 7th Lord Greystoke (Tarzan's father). The 'Clayton' surname is family; Greystoke is the peerage title. The mother ape Kala raises Tarzan. The Tarzan-of-the-Apes book appeared in 1914. Johnny Weissmuller's 1932 MGM film cemented the iconic image.

question: A 1928 H.P. Lovecraft story published in Weird Tales introduced a sleeping cosmic entity beneath a sunken Pacific city called R'lyeh, brought to wider attention through a Louisiana cult raid and a Norwegian sailor's manuscript. What was the story called?
context: Published in the February 1928 Weird Tales. The story is told in three parts via the papers of Professor George Gammell Angell of Brown University. The Cthulhu mythos vocabulary — R'lyeh, the Necronomicon, the cult phrase 'In his house at R'lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming' — all enter the canon here.

question: Frank Herbert's Dune (1965) was rejected by twenty publishers before a Philadelphia auto-manuals company took a chance on it. The protagonist is Paul Atreides, heir to a noble house exiled to a brutal desert planet. What's the planet officially called?
context: Arrakis is colloquially called Dune. The desert is the only source of spice melange — the substance that enables faster-than-light navigation across the Imperium. The native Fremen people drink water-of-life and ride sandworms called Shai-Hulud.

question: An 1894 short story by the Welsh writer Arthur Machen about a young woman whose god-encounter on a Welsh hillside leaves her insane and gives birth to a daughter capable of driving men to suicide was a major influence on Lovecraft. What was the story?
context: Machen lived 1863-1947. The Great God Pan was published by John Lane in 1894 to scandal — Victorian readers found its sexual implications horrifying. Lovecraft listed it as one of the greatest horror stories ever written in his 1927 essay 'Supernatural Horror in Literature.' Stephen King has called it 'maybe the best [horror story] in the English language.'

question: Tolkien's posthumous 1977 book of First Age myths covering the creation of Middle-earth, the fall of Morgoth, and the legendary jewels was edited from his unfinished manuscripts. Who edited it?
context: Christopher Tolkien (1924-2020) was J.R.R.'s third son and literary executor. He spent the rest of his life editing his father's papers — twelve volumes of The History of Middle-earth (1983-1996) plus Unfinished Tales (1980), The Children of Húrin (2007), Beren and Lúthien (2017), and The Fall of Gondolin (2018). Guy Gavriel Kay assisted on The Silmarillion.

question: Fritz Leiber's 1939 short story 'Two Sought Adventure' introduced two roguish swords-for-hire — a giant northern barbarian and a small thief-magician's apprentice — in a corrupt city called Lankhmar. What were the two heroes called?
context: The story appeared in Unknown magazine in August 1939. Leiber coined the term 'sword and sorcery' in 1961 to describe the genre Howard had founded. The Fafhrd & Mouser series ran across 35+ tales and seven volumes through the 1980s, with Leiber writing into his 80s.

question: A 1961 Michael Moorcock novella in Science Fantasy magazine introduced an albino sorcerer-emperor of a decadent magical race, dependent on drugs and a sentient black sword that drinks souls. The character became a foundational anti-hero of dark fantasy. What's the sorcerer's name?
context: Elric's sword is Stormbringer. Moorcock developed the larger concept of the Eternal Champion (Elric, Corum, Hawkmoon, Erekosë, etc.) — different incarnations of the same hero across multiple worlds. The original Elric stories ran 1961-1964 in Science Fantasy; Moorcock has returned to the character repeatedly since.

question: An 1843 short story by Edgar Allan Poe set during the Spanish Inquisition has a prisoner strapped to a board beneath a swinging blade and a closing iron-walled chamber. What's the story called?
choices: The Masque of the Red Death
context: Published in the 1842 Gift annual. The narrator is sentenced by the Inquisition, escapes the central pit, then is bound under a pendulum scything closer with each swing. The story ends with French troops arriving — General Lasalle has taken Toledo. Poe's view of the Inquisition was a major influence on later gothic fiction.

question: Robert Heinlein's 1959 novel about powered armor, mobile infantry training, and a war against giant arachnid aliens of Klendathu won the Hugo Award and was adapted (controversially) into a 1997 Paul Verhoeven film. What was the novel called?
choices: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
context: Heinlein conceived powered armor (the Mobile Infantry suits) in the novel, influencing every mecha and powered-armor concept since. The book's political philosophy — full citizenship earned only through federal service — provoked decades of debate. Verhoeven's 1997 film satirized the politics; Heinlein's text plays them straight.

question: Howard's pulp competitor in 1928 introduced a Puritan adventurer in slouch hat and rapier who wanders the world battling the supernatural and avenging the innocent. The character is Howard's grim-religious counterpoint to the pagan Conan. What's his name?
context: Solomon Kane debuted in 'Red Shadows' in Weird Tales, August 1928 — four years before Conan. He is older than Conan by composition; Howard envisioned him as an Elizabethan-era Englishman in his sixties. The 2009 Michael J. Bassett film starred James Purefoy. Howard wrote ten Solomon Kane stories.

question: Tolkien and C.S. Lewis were members of an informal Oxford literary group that met for years in pubs and at Lewis's college rooms, reading drafts of works in progress including The Hobbit and Narnia. What was the group called?
context: The Inklings included Lewis, Tolkien, Charles Williams, Owen Barfield, Hugo Dyson, and Lewis's brother Warnie. They met at the Eagle and Child pub (nicknamed the Bird and Baby) on St. Giles' Street, Oxford. Tolkien read drafts of LOTR to the group; Lewis read drafts of Narnia and Out of the Silent Planet.

question: From 1920 to 1951, a pulp magazine called Black Mask was the principal home of hardboiled detective fiction in America, publishing Hammett, Chandler, Erle Stanley Gardner, and Cornell Woolrich. Hammett's most famous Black Mask serial protagonist was a nameless agent. What was he called?
context: The Continental Op (short for 'Operative') works for the Continental Detective Agency, modeled on Hammett's real Pinkerton service. The Op appeared in 36 stories and the novels Red Harvest (1929) and The Dain Curse (1929). He is short, stout, middle-aged, and unnamed throughout.

question: Lovecraft's most famous fictional book — invented in his stories but believed by countless readers to be real — is supposedly the work of an 'Mad Arab' named Abdul Alhazred. What is the book called?
context: Lovecraft invented the Necronomicon for his story 'The Hound' (1922). Multiple actual published 'Necronomicons' (Simon's 1977, Wilson's 1978) exist as hoaxes. Libraries still receive inquiries from people convinced the book is real. Lovecraft wrote a mock 'History of the Necronomicon' (1927) detailing the imaginary book's transmission.

question: August Derleth founded a small publishing house in Sauk City, Wisconsin in 1939 specifically to preserve Lovecraft's work after Lovecraft's death two years earlier. The house has remained in continuous operation since. What's the press called?
context: Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House to publish The Outsider and Others (1939), the first major Lovecraft collection. Without Derleth, Lovecraft's work might have disappeared into pulp obscurity. Derleth also wrote his own Cthulhu Mythos stories, often controversial among Lovecraft scholars for systematizing what Lovecraft had left ambiguous.

question: Philip K. Dick's 1962 alternate-history novel imagined a world where the Axis won World War II and Japan and Germany divided North America. The book centers on a novel-within-the-novel called The Grasshopper Lies Heavy. What was Dick's outer novel called?
answer: The Man in the High Castle
choices: The Man in the High Castle
Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said
context: Won the 1963 Hugo Award. Dick used the I Ching to make plot decisions while writing. The story is set in 1962 in a Japanese-occupied West Coast (PSA), with a German-occupied East and a neutral Rocky Mountain States buffer. Hawthorne Abendsen is the in-novel author of Grasshopper, the inverse alternate-history showing an Allied victory.

question: A 1922 epic fantasy by the English diplomat Eric Rücker Eddison features a war between the demons of Demonland and the witches of Witchland over a Mercury that is not the planet. Tolkien admired the prose but found it morally confused. What was the novel called?
context: Eddison's prose imitates the cadence of Jacobean drama; he had translated Egil's Saga from the Old Norse. Tolkien wrote that Eddison was 'the greatest and most convincing writer of invented worlds I have read' but disliked his Nietzschean ethics. The 'worm' (Old English word for dragon) circles back on itself — the story's ending loops to its beginning.

question: Robert E. Howard wrote his Conan stories between 1932 and 1935 in his bedroom in his parents' Cross Plains house. He typed his stories on a Royal portable, often barefoot, dictating dialogue aloud to test the rhythm. He once explained to a friend in a letter that Conan was so vivid he felt the barbarian was 'standing at my shoulder' compelling him to write. Who was that friend correspondent — the man who became Howard's primary literary confidant from 1930 until Howard's death?
context: The Howard-Lovecraft correspondence (1930-1936) survives in roughly 200 letters totaling around 600,000 words. They never met in person. Their core argument was over the merits of civilization vs. barbarism — Howard the Texan defender of frontier vigor, Lovecraft the New England civilizationist. Howard's suicide devastated Lovecraft.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's 1936 novella, his longest single work, follows an Antarctic geological expedition from Miskatonic University that discovers pre-human ruins under the ice and the remains of a barrel-shaped, star-headed extraterrestrial civilization that built those ruins millions of years ago. The story was first published serialized in Astounding Stories. What was the title?
choices: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward
context: Astounding ran it across the February, March, and April 1936 issues — Lovecraft's only appearance in that magazine. The Elder Things (the barrel-shaped beings) carved 'shoggoths' — protoplasmic slave creatures — that eventually overthrew their masters. The Antarctic setting drew on the contemporary Byrd Antarctic Expedition (1928-1930). Guillermo del Toro has been trying to film it for over twenty years.

question: The Phoenix on the Sword, Robert E. Howard's first Conan story published in Weird Tales December 1932, was actually a rewrite of an earlier rejected Howard story featuring his older creation King Kull. Kull was an Atlantean barbarian who became king of which fallen civilization?
context: Kull debuted in 'The Shadow Kingdom' (Weird Tales, August 1929). Valusia is the most powerful of the Seven Empires of Howard's pre-Cataclysm world. Kull and the snake-people of Valusia inspired numerous later writers including Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp. Conan's Hyborian Age is technically a later epoch after Kull's Atlantis sinks.

question: Clark Ashton Smith — the third member of the Weird Tales triumvirate alongside Howard and Lovecraft — lived as a near-recluse in a small cabin in California, writing fewer stories than his peers but with more elaborate prose. His best-known cycle is set in Zothique, the last continent of a dying far-future Earth. In what California town did Smith spend most of his life?
context: Smith (1893-1961) lived in a self-built cabin near Auburn, California. He was a teenage prodigy poet first, then turned to weird fiction in the late 1920s. His Zothique, Hyperborea, Averoigne, and Xiccarph cycles each represent different fantastic milieus. Smith ground his own pigments and carved fantastic stone heads in his last years. His correspondence with Lovecraft was nearly as substantial as Howard's.

question: Tolkien's invented Elvish languages — which he developed for decades before The Lord of the Rings was even conceived — fall into two main branches. The high-speech of the Noldor Elves (used in formal contexts in LOTR) was meant to sound like Latin or Finnish. The everyday speech of the Sindar Elves (used for most Elvish names in LOTR) was meant to sound like Welsh. Name those two languages.
context: Tolkien was a philology professor at Oxford whose academic work centered on Old English and the West Midlands dialect. He created Quenya around 1915 based on Finnish phonology after reading the Kalevala. Sindarin's Welsh-style consonant mutations come from Tolkien's love of Welsh place-names. Khuzdul (Dwarvish, modeled on Semitic languages) is heard rarely; the Black Speech of Mordor was created by Sauron.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published a long narrative poem in 1849, four months before his mysterious death in Baltimore. The poem opens 'It was many and many a year ago, in a kingdom by the sea, that a maiden there lived whom you may know by the name of...' — the title is the maiden's name. What is it?
context: Poe's wife Virginia Clemm — whom he married when she was 13 and he was 27 — had died of tuberculosis on January 30, 1847 in their Bronx cottage. Annabel Lee is widely read as a memorial to her, though Poe also referenced his earlier crushes. Poe himself died October 7, 1849 in Baltimore under circumstances still debated; he was found wandering, delirious, in someone else's clothing. The poem was first published two days later.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs invented a series of subterranean novels about a hollow Earth accessed near the North Pole, where dinosaurs survive and primitive humans wage wars with stone tools. The world is lit by an inner sun and has no concept of time. What did Burroughs call this hollow-Earth realm?
context: At the Earth's Core (1914) opens the Pellucidar series; Burroughs wrote seven Pellucidar novels through 1944. David Innes and his mentor Abner Perry tunnel down into the inner world in a mechanical 'iron mole.' The Caspak series (The Land That Time Forgot, 1918) is a separate Burroughs lost-world setup involving a Pacific island, not hollow Earth. Tarzan visits Pellucidar in a 1929 crossover.

question: John W. Campbell's Astounding under his editorship saw the debut publication of Isaac Asimov, Robert Heinlein, Theodore Sturgeon, A.E. van Vogt, Lester del Rey, and L. Ron Hubbard. Asimov's first sale to Campbell was an October 1939 story about a robot named Robbie who serves as a child's nanny — the seed of Asimov's robot stories and the famous Three Laws. What was the story originally titled when published?
context: Strange Playfellow appeared in Super Science Stories (September 1940), not Astounding — Campbell had rejected it. Asimov retitled the story 'Robbie' when he collected it in I, Robot (1950). The Three Laws of Robotics were formalized in 'Runaround' (March 1942 Astounding). Asimov's first Campbell sale was 'Marooned Off Vesta' to Amazing Stories, not Astounding.

question: Tolkien's 'On Fairy-Stories' is the most important theoretical statement of his approach to fantasy. He delivered it as an Andrew Lang lecture at the University of St Andrews in 1939 and published it in revised form in a 1947 collection. The essay coined or refined a term Tolkien used for the redemptive happy ending of a story — the unexpected turn of joy. What is that term?
context: Eucatastrophe = 'good catastrophe.' Tolkien argued the Gospels are the eucatastrophe of human history — Christ's resurrection being the supreme unexpected turn from death to life. The essay also developed 'sub-creation' (the artist as imitator of God's creative act) and the primary/secondary world distinction. It first appeared in the 1947 Essays Presented to Charles Williams memorial volume.

question: Lovecraft's 1929 story set in the rural Massachusetts town of Dunwich features the Whateley family of degenerate hill-folk, the boy Wilbur who is half human and half cosmic horror, and his invisible brother. The story climaxes with three Miskatonic professors using arcane defenses on Sentinel Hill. What's the story?
context: Published in Weird Tales, April 1929. Wilbur Whateley's father is the cosmic entity Yog-Sothoth; his mother is the albino Lavinia Whateley. The 'horror' itself is Wilbur's invisible twin brother, kept in the family farmhouse. Stuart Gordon's 1970 AIP film starring Dean Stockwell and Sandra Dee adapted it. The Necronomicon plays a key role in the climax.

question: Lester Dent's Doc Savage was supported by five specialists nicknamed the Fabulous Five: Monk Mayfair the chemist, Ham Brooks the lawyer, Renny Renwick the engineer, Long Tom Roberts the electrical wizard, and Johnny Littlejohn the geologist. Doc was raised from infancy to be a physical and mental superman by a team his father hired. According to Dent's canon, where was Doc actually born?
answer: During a hurricane at sea on a schooner
choices: During a hurricane at sea on a schooner
In Hidalgo, his secret Central American haven
In Manhattan, in his father's hospital suite
In the Yucatan, in his father's Mayan refuge
context: Doc Savage's full name is Clark Savage Jr. His father Clark Savage Sr. arranged his unique upbringing. The Hidalgo Trust funds his adventures from a hidden Central American valley. Doc's HQ was on the 86th floor of a New York skyscraper modeled on the Empire State Building. Marvel published Doc Savage comics in 1972; George Pal directed a 1975 film flop.

question: Robert Heinlein, Isaac Asimov, and L. Sprague de Camp all spent World War II working in the same building — the Philadelphia Naval Yard — on materials-science problems related to high-altitude aircraft. The trio became lifelong friends and wrote stories about their wartime work. What was the name of the navy facility?
context: Heinlein, Asimov, and de Camp worked on aviation rubber, gasket sealing, and altitude-suit engineering at the Naval Aircraft Materials Laboratory (then in Philadelphia, later moved to NADC Johnsville) from 1942 to 1945. Heinlein had been Navy regular until tuberculosis discharged him in 1934. The three wrote up their pranks and the science culture in various memoirs. Asimov used the experience for the laboratory sections of his Foundation and Robot stories.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1839 short story features a melancholy nobleman in a crumbling ancestral house above a stagnant tarn, his cataleptic sister whom he buries alive (he later admits) in the family vault, and the literal collapse of the house at the climax. What's the story called?
answer: The Fall of the House of Usher
choices: The Fall of the House of Usher
context: Published in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, September 1839. The narrator visits his old friend Roderick Usher and witnesses the unraveling of the Usher line. The 'House' is both the physical mansion and the family bloodline. Roger Corman directed the 1960 AIP adaptation with Vincent Price — the first of Corman's eight Poe-cycle films. Debussy and Glass have both attempted operas of the story.

question: L. Sprague de Camp and Lin Carter were the most important Conan continuators after Howard's 1936 death. From the 1950s into the 1980s, they edited Howard's manuscripts, completed his unfinished Conan fragments, and wrote new Conan novels of their own. De Camp's 1953 edited collection — the first paperback Conan revival — was published by which company?
context: Gnome Press's Conan the Conqueror (1950) was the first hardback Conan. De Camp's Tales of Conan (1955) added pastiche stories. The Lancer paperback editions (1966-1971), with Frank Frazetta covers, made Conan into a cultural phenomenon and inspired the 1970s sword-and-sorcery boom. Frazetta's painting for Conan the Adventurer (1966) sold for $1.4M in 2018.

question: Tolkien's invented script for writing Quenya and Sindarin uses 24 basic letters arranged on a grid of voiced/unvoiced and stop/continuant consonants — a system Tolkien designed phonetically rather than alphabetically. The script appears on the One Ring's inscription and on Moria's western gate ('Speak, friend, and enter'). What's the script called?
context: Tengwar means 'letters' in Quenya. Tolkien invented it in the 1930s. Cirth is a separate runic alphabet used by the Dwarves for stone-cutting. The One Ring inscription is in Tengwar letters but renders the Black Speech of Mordor — 'Ash nazg durbatulûk, ash nazg gimbatul...' Tolkien also invented the Sarati (an earlier elvish script) and various tengwar modes for different languages.

question: Edgar Allan Poe died in Baltimore on October 7, 1849, four days after he was found delirious, wearing someone else's clothes, outside Ryan's Tavern. His death has remained mysterious for over 175 years. He was repeatedly heard to call out a name in his hospital delirium. What name?
context: No 'Reynolds' connected to Poe has ever been definitively identified — Jeremiah Reynolds, the Antarctic explorer Poe had once championed, is one candidate. The 'cooping' theory holds that Poe was kidnapped by political operatives, plied with alcohol, and forced to vote multiple times at different polls (election day was October 3); the 'rabies' theory was proposed in 1996 by R. Michael Benitez. Whitman, Baudelaire, and Mallarmé all wrote in defense of Poe's reputation after attacks by his literary executor Rufus Griswold.

question: A 1933 pulp magazine series by Walter Gibson, writing as Maxwell Grant, featured a master-of-disguise vigilante and his network of agents fighting crime in New York. The Shadow's secret identity in canon was a wealthy man-about-town — though the radio show changed this to a different alias. What name does the pulp Shadow primarily use as cover?
context: Kent Allard is the pulp Shadow's 'real' identity — a former World War I pilot called the Black Eagle who faked his death in 1918. Lamont Cranston is one of Allard's many cover identities; the radio show (which Orson Welles narrated 1937-38) made Cranston the principal identity. Gibson wrote 282 Shadow novels at a pace of two per month from 1931 to 1949.

question: Tolkien's 1949 short story (and posthumous novel sourcework) tells of an Anglo-Saxon Earendel-figure, a man whose painting of a great Tree is constantly interrupted by tasks for neighbors. He dies before finishing and finds the actual Tree of his dreams in the afterlife. The story is Tolkien's most direct allegory of his own creative struggles. What is the story called?
context: Leaf by Niggle was first published in the Dublin Review (January 1945) alongside 'On Fairy-Stories' in the 1964 Tree and Leaf collection. Niggle is a not-very-good painter constantly distracted by his neighbor Parish. The story is read as a parable of art, purgatory, and the Beatific Vision. Tolkien said he wrote it 'in a single sitting' after a worried dream. Theologians have noted strong Dante influence.

question: Lord Dunsany — the Anglo-Irish baron Edward Plunkett — published a 1905 book of invented mythology that became a primary influence on Lovecraft and Tolkien. The book describes the gods of a fictional pantheon in formal, archaic prose modeled on the King James Bible. What was the book called?
context: The Gods of Pegana (1905) was followed by Time and the Gods (1906) and many short-story collections through the 1940s. Lovecraft's Dream Cycle stories (e.g., The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) are direct Dunsany homages. Tolkien acknowledged Dunsany's prose-style influence on his early Silmarillion drafts. The King of Elfland's Daughter (1924) is Dunsany's most-read fantasy novel today.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published his only complete novel in 1838 — a strange seafaring narrative full of mutiny, starvation, cannibalism, and a southern-polar voyage ending in a sudden white apparition. Jules Verne wrote a sequel to it; Lovecraft drew on it for At the Mountains of Madness. What was the novel called?
answer: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
choices: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
context: Pym was published by Harper & Brothers in July 1838. The novel's last lines describe a white shrouded figure in the polar sea — Lovecraft used the cry 'Tekeli-li!' from the novel as the cry of the shoggoths in Mountains of Madness. Jules Verne's 1897 sequel was An Antarctic Mystery (Le Sphinx des glaces). Borges wrote that Pym's final whiteness was the model for Moby-Dick's whiteness chapter.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's 1931 story (rejected by Weird Tales and not published until 1936) involves a Massachusetts coastal town where the inhabitants have interbred with sea-creatures from a sunken reef offshore. The narrator escapes but eventually realizes his own ancestry. What's the town called?
context: The Shadow Over Innsmouth was published in 1936 by Visionary Publishing in a 200-copy print run — the only Lovecraft book published in his lifetime. The sea-creatures are the Deep Ones, servants of Father Dagon and Mother Hydra. Innsmouth's reef is Devil Reef offshore. Robert Eggers's 2024 film Nosferatu and several of Stephen King's stories nod to Innsmouth lore.

question: Tolkien's prose romance posthumously edited and released in 2007 by Christopher Tolkien tells the doomed story of a cursed Mannish hero in the First Age, his accidental marriage to his own sister, and his suicide on a black sword that addresses him in Sindarin. What was that 2007 publication called?
context: The Children of Húrin (Narn i Hîn Húrin) is the central tragic tale of the First Age. The hero is Túrin Turambar; his sword is Anglachel/Gurthang. Christopher Tolkien assembled the novel from JRRT's manuscripts and added a frame structure. Alan Lee illustrated the 2007 edition. The story is Tolkien's most explicit homage to the Finnish Kalevala's Kullervo cycle.

question: On the evening of June 10, 1936, in Cross Plains, Texas, Robert E. Howard's mother Hester had been bedridden with tuberculosis for years. She fell into her final coma that afternoon. Howard asked the night nurse whether his mother would ever speak again; when she said no, Howard left the bedroom, walked outside to his 1935 Chevrolet sedan parked in the driveway, sat in the driver's seat, took out a .380 Colt pistol his father had been keeping locked away, and shot himself in the head. He lived about eight hours after the shot. He had typed out a couplet that morning that he left on his typewriter, beginning 'All fled, all done.' What was the couplet's source — the line he had once quoted in a letter as the proper epitaph for a Texan?
choices: An original couplet Howard composed for his own grave
A line from Howard's own 1929 poem 'The King and the Oak'
An anonymous couplet from a 1934 issue of Weird Tales
context: The full couplet was 'All fled, all done, so lift me on the pyre; the feast is over and the lamps expire.' Howard had quoted Viola Garvin's poem (published 1932 in the British periodical John O'London's Weekly) in his correspondence with H.P. Lovecraft. Hester Howard died about thirty hours after her son, on June 12, 1936. Both were buried in the same Cross Plains plot. Howard was 30, his mother 66.

question: H.P. Lovecraft died on March 15, 1937 in Providence's Jane Brown Memorial Hospital of intestinal cancer that had spread beyond treatment. He had been keeping detailed medical notes in a diary because he was curious about his own symptoms. His estate at death amounted to roughly $25. Two young readers and correspondents — devastated by his death — founded a small Wisconsin press in 1939 specifically to keep his work in print. They published his first hardback collection that year, securing his legacy. Who were the two founders?
choices: Frank Belknap Long and Clark Ashton Smith
Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp
context: Arkham House's first publication was The Outsider and Others (1939) — 1,268 copies, edited by Derleth and Wandrei from Lovecraft's manuscripts in Lovecraft's widow Sonia's possession. The press is named for Lovecraft's fictional New England city. Without Derleth and Wandrei's salvage operation, Lovecraft might have remained pulp-obscure. Derleth himself wrote dozens of mythos pastiches afterward, often criticized for systematizing what Lovecraft had left ambiguous. Wandrei was a poet and stockbroker, less prolific.

question: John W. Campbell took over Astounding Stories in October 1937 and renamed it Astounding Science-Fiction in early 1938. Over the next decade, he published the debut or early stories of every major Golden Age writer except Bradbury. Campbell paid above-market rates for the era (1 cent per word, sometimes 2). He famously bought a 1939 short story from a Brooklyn College student who had written it under the pen name 'Don A. Stuart' — but the byline was actually Campbell's own pseudonym, used for a 1934 story he had pre-Campbell. The 1939 sale that broke the new writer's career was not the same as the pseudonym confusion. That Brooklyn College student was a teenager when he sold his first story to Campbell. Who was he?
context: Asimov's first Campbell sale was 'Trends' (Astounding, July 1939) — he was 19. The Don A. Stuart pen name was Campbell's, used for stories like 'Twilight' (1934) and 'Who Goes There?' (1938) — the rationale was to write quietly literary stories that contrasted with his loud pulp 'Campbell' style. Heinlein's first sale to Campbell was 'Life-Line' (Astounding, August 1939) — one month after Asimov's debut. Both became Campbell's two flagship writers.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs founded his own publishing company in 1923 — frustrated with what he considered insufficient royalties from established publishers — and personally incorporated as a corporation under California law, becoming arguably the first author to do so. By the late 1930s, his California estate at Tarzana was both his home and his corporate headquarters. The town of Tarzana, California (annexed by Los Angeles in 1936) actually took its name from his estate. Burroughs died on March 19, 1950, having sold over 100 million copies in his lifetime. His company is still publishing him. What was the corporate name?
context: Burroughs incorporated as a corporation on March 17, 1923. He had been writing for All-Story / Argosy under the pen name 'Normal Bean' (his Tarzan debut byline) since 1911. His Tarzana estate covered 540 acres of the San Fernando Valley; the town of Tarzana now houses 36,000 people. Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc. is still owned by the family and licenses both Tarzan and the Mars/John Carter franchises. The 2012 Disney film John Carter was a major flop but is now a cult film.

question: Tolkien served in the Lancashire Fusiliers as a signals officer in 1916. He was sent to France in early June. By July 1 he was on the Somme front. He fought at Thiepval and Beaumont-Hamel. He contracted trench fever (a louse-borne illness, not as deadly as typhus or flu but debilitating) in late October and was invalided back to England on November 8, 1916. Of his four-member Oxford school club — the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society) — three were killed during the war. Two of them died in 1916 during the Somme campaign Tolkien himself fought in. What were those two T.C.B.S. friends' names?
answer: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
choices: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
Hugh Cary Gilson and Edward Williams
context: Rob Gilson was killed at La Boisselle on July 1, 1916 — the first day of the Somme. G.B. Smith died on December 3, 1916 of gangrene from a shell wound. The fourth T.C.B.S. member, Christopher Wiseman, survived the war. Tolkien edited Smith's poetry (A Spring Harvest, 1918) after his death. His Silmarillion mythology had been gestating since 1914; the war crystallized his sense of what fantasy was for. Charles Williams and Owen Barfield were later Inklings associates, not the T.C.B.S.

question: Frank Herbert worked for ten years on Dune before its 1965 hardcover publication by Chilton Books — a Philadelphia firm primarily known for publishing auto-repair manuals. The novel had been rejected by twenty publishers, including all the major science-fiction houses (Doubleday, Putnam, Ace, etc.). Herbert had originally researched Dune as a magazine article about Oregon's dunes and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's effort to use beach grass to stabilize them. He had a working title for the book that he eventually rejected as too on-the-nose. What was the working title?
context: The Spice Planet was a shorter early draft (1958) that Herbert later expanded into the full Dune novel; the original draft survived and was reconstructed by Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson in 2005. Herbert's 1957 magazine article 'They Stopped the Moving Sands' was the project's seed. The Chilton hardcover went almost unnoticed at first; Ace Books's 1967 paperback made it a bestseller. Dune won both the Hugo (1966) and the inaugural Nebula (1966) — the first novel to win both.

question: Philip K. Dick wrote 44 novels between 1955 and his death in March 1982 — five months before Ridley Scott's Blade Runner premiered. Many of his last novels were drug-influenced and autobiographical. His 1981 novel about a divine encounter following a 1974 mystical episode was deeply influenced by what Dick called the 'Black Iron Prison' theory of reality. The novel takes its title from a four-letter acronym for the godlike intelligence. What was the 1981 novel called?
context: VALIS stands for Vast Active Living Intelligence System. The novel is the first of Dick's so-called VALIS Trilogy, with two 1982 companion books. VALIS is rooted in Dick's February-March 1974 experiences — what he called 2-3-74 — which he believed were either spiritual experiences, schizophrenic episodes, or signals from an alien-divine intelligence. He filled an 8,000-page Exegesis trying to understand them; a selection was published posthumously in 2011.

question: Tolkien wrote The Hobbit largely between 1930 and 1932 during his time as Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford. The book famously opens with a line he scribbled on the back of an exam paper he was grading. He didn't know what a 'hobbit' was at the time — the word came first. The exam paper was for the School Certificate Examination in English. What was the opening line he scribbled?
answer: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
choices: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
Far over the misty mountains cold
There was once a hobbit who lived in a hole
Bilbo Baggins of Bag End was no ordinary hobbit
context: Tolkien said the line came to him 'out of nowhere' while he was looking at a blank examination booklet. He set it aside and only returned to writing the book around 1932. He read drafts aloud to his children. C.S. Lewis read it in manuscript around 1933 and pushed him to finish it. Susan Dagnall at George Allen & Unwin recommended publication. The first edition (September 21, 1937) had a print run of 1,500 copies.

question: Manly Wade Wellman was a 1930s pulp writer who became, in his second career, the leading practitioner of American folklore-horror fiction. From 1951 onward he wrote the John the Balladeer (or 'Silver John') stories — set in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina, featuring a wandering Korean War veteran with a silver-stringed guitar who confronts witches, devils, and dark fae rooted in actual Appalachian folklore. Wellman's silver-stringed-guitar conceit was rooted in real American folk-music tradition. He wrote his first Silver John story for which 1951 fantasy magazine?
answer: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
choices: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
Weird Tales after the Wright era end
Unknown Worlds, the Campbell sister title
Beyond Fantasy Fiction, the Galaxy spinoff
context: Wellman's 'O Ugly Bird!' appeared in F&SF in December 1951. The Silver John stories are characteristically narrated in first-person mountain dialect. Wellman won the British Fantasy Society's August Derleth Award (1975) for Worse Things Waiting; he also won the World Fantasy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1980. He died in 1986 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina at age 82. His Silver John novels include After Dark (1980) and The Lost and the Lurking (1981).

question: Karl Edward Wagner — a North Carolina physician-turned-writer and 1970s editor of the Year's Best Horror Stories anthology — created an immortal red-haired swordsman who is the literal Cain of Genesis, marked by God after killing his brother and condemned to wander Earth forever. Wagner's character debuted in a 1970 small-press novel and ran across roughly fifteen stories before Wagner's 1994 death. What was the character's name?
context: Kane's first novel Darkness Weaves was Wagner's 1970 debut with Powell Books. Wagner combined sword-and-sorcery with cosmic horror and biblical apocrypha. Kane is the original Cain, his red hair the mark God set upon him. The character is amoral and brilliant — Wagner explicitly rejected the heroic-fantasy mode of Howard or Tolkien. Kane novels include Bloodstone (1975), Dark Crusade (1976), and The Book of Kane (1985). Wagner died of alcoholism aged 48 in October 1994.

question: William Hope Hodgson wrote four major weird-fiction novels in the early 1900s before his death at Ypres in 1918 (he was 40, killed by a German artillery shell during the Battle of Mont Kemmel). His most cosmically ambitious novel, published 1912, is set far in the future on an Earth where the sun has gone dark and the last refuge of humanity is a colossal pyramid-fortress called the Last Redoubt, surrounded by monstrous creatures from beyond the lightless world. What was the novel called?
choices: The Boats of the Glen Carrig
context: The Night Land's prose imitates 17th-century English deliberately — Hodgson considered it formal scriptural style appropriate to the eschatological subject. The novel was reviewed unenthusiastically in 1912 but became a major influence on Lovecraft (who called it 'one of the most potent pieces of macabre imagination ever written'), Clark Ashton Smith, and later Gene Wolfe. Hodgson was a former merchant-marine officer; the sea-horror in his earlier novels The Boats of the Glen Carrig (1907) and The Ghost Pirates (1909) drew from his own North Atlantic experience.

question: Algernon Blackwood — the English fantasist and Society for Psychical Research investigator — published a 1907 novella widely considered one of the greatest weird stories ever written. Two friends canoeing down the Danube River in a wild section of central Europe (the borderland between Hungary and the Balkans) camp on a sandbar overgrown with thick willow trees. They begin to sense that the willows are watching them — and that something on the other side of the natural world is trying to break through. Lovecraft, in his 1927 essay on horror in literature, ranked it as the single finest piece of weird fiction he had ever read. What was the story called?
context: The Willows was published in The Listener and Other Stories (1907). Blackwood himself had canoed the Danube in 1900. His other major weird stories include The Wendigo (1910, the source of the modern North American Wendigo mythos in popular culture) and the John Silence stories — proto-psychic-investigator tales. Blackwood lived 1869-1951 and became a BBC radio personality in his later years, reading his own ghost stories on Christmas broadcasts.

question: M.R. (Montague Rhodes) James was a medieval scholar and Provost of Eton (later Cambridge's King's College) who wrote ghost stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas. He published four collections between 1904 and 1925. His stories defined what is now called the 'antiquarian ghost story' — bookish scholars, ancient artifacts, dusty cathedral libraries, slow-building dread. His 1911 collection includes a story about a Cambridge professor who pulls a strange bronze whistle out of a Roman ruin and finds something is now following him through the empty seaside hotel where he is staying. What was the story called?
answer: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
choices: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
The Treasure of Abbot Thomas (1904 tale)
Count Magnus and the Black Pilgrim Tale
context: Oh, Whistle was published in More Ghost Stories of an Antiquary (1911). The professor is named Parkins; the hotel is in the fictional Burnstow on the East Anglian coast. The story has been adapted twice by the BBC (1968 starring Michael Hordern, 2010 starring John Hurt). The whistle bears the Latin inscription 'Quis est iste qui venit' — 'Who is this who is coming?' James's collected stories were a major influence on H.P. Lovecraft and continue to be read aloud at Christmas in many English households.

question: On October 8, 1928 — three months before The Call of Cthulhu went to print — H.P. Lovecraft sat down to write a letter to Frank Belknap Long describing a story idea he had just had. The story would feature an Arkham professor whose vacation home in rural Vermont becomes the focus of a winged-crustacean alien race who mine for a metal called Tok'l. The aliens have a particular use for human brains, which they preserve in metal cylinders to carry their consciousness through interstellar travel. The story Lovecraft was incubating became, when published in Weird Tales in August 1930, his most overt science-fiction-horror hybrid. What was the story called?
choices: The Dreams in the Witch House
context: The aliens are the Mi-go (the Lovecraft-canon name for the Yuggoth Outer Ones), fungoid-crustacean entities that mine Vermont for rare minerals. They preserve a fugitive man's brain in a metal cylinder so it can converse from beyond the body. The story is set in the wake of the November 1927 Vermont floods, a real historical event. The 2011 H.P. Lovecraft Historical Society silent-film adaptation is considered the most accurate Lovecraft film made.

question: Tolkien's invented language for the Dwarves — Khuzdul — is a secret language the Dwarves rarely share with outsiders. Tolkien based its phonology on Semitic languages (Hebrew especially), in contrast to his Indo-European Elvish languages. Khuzdul has only a few surviving words in The Lord of the Rings, including the Dwarvish names for places and the war-cry the Dwarves use against the Balrog in the Mines of Moria during Gimli's outburst at Balin's tomb. What was that war-cry?
context: The cry translates as 'Axes of the Dwarves! The Dwarves are upon you!' Tolkien designed Khuzdul phonetically to feel angular and stone-like, matching the Dwarves' culture. The Dwarves' true names (in Khuzdul) are kept secret from outsiders; the names we know (Thorin, Balin, Gimli, etc.) are Mannish translations from a related Northern-Mannish tongue. Tolkien based the secret-language idea partly on Hebrew traditions about the Tetragrammaton.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published his first detective story — and arguably invented the genre — in Graham's Lady's and Gentleman's Magazine in April 1841. The narrator's friend, a brilliant impoverished aristocrat, solves the locked-room murder of two women whose injuries no human assailant could plausibly have inflicted. Conan Doyle would later acknowledge the story as the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes. The two murdered women were named in the story. What was their family name?
context: Madame and Mademoiselle L'Espanaye are murdered in The Murders in the Rue Morgue, the first Dupin story. The actual killer turns out to be an escaped orangutan from a Maltese sailor. Poe followed it with The Mystery of Marie Rogêt (1842) and The Purloined Letter (1844) — three Dupin stories total. Conan Doyle wrote in his autobiography Memories and Adventures (1924) that Sherlock Holmes was a direct descendant of Dupin, with Poe holding 'the master's place.'

question: Howard's bone-deep historical knowledge informed his lesser-known but possibly best work — his series about a Pictish king of post-Roman Britain who defies the imperial cohorts. The character was Howard's pre-Conan attempt at literary historical fantasy, and Howard wrote eight stories about him from 1926 to 1932. The Picts are a real ancient people of northern Britain; Howard's character is their dying king, fighting the encroaching Roman empire. What was the character's name?
context: Bran's signature story is 'Worms of the Earth' (Weird Tales, November 1932) — Bran descends into prehistoric darkness to call on a degenerate subterranean race to destroy a Roman governor. Howard's Bran stories appeared between 1926 and 1932. The Picts in Howard's mythos are the longest-running race; they survive into Conan's Hyborian Age as the savage forest-tribes of the West. Lovecraft praised 'Worms of the Earth' as Howard's finest single story.

question: Tolkien wrote thousands of letters about Middle-earth. His longest correspondence about his own published work was with Milton Waldman, an editor at Collins who briefly considered publishing The Silmarillion alongside LOTR in 1951. Tolkien's December 1951 letter to Waldman runs over 10,000 words and is the single best statement of the mythology's deeper themes. Tolkien identified one fall-from-grace pattern as the engine driving all of his Middle-earth tragedy — Fëanor, Sauron, Saruman, Boromir, and the Numenoreans all share it. What did Tolkien call this pattern in the letter?
answer: The desire of the lover for the Beloved Subcreated Thing made his own possession
choices: The desire of the lover for the Beloved Subcreated Thing made his own possession
The temptation by which industrial machinery destroys the bearer's soul
The biblical sin of pride straightforwardly imported from Genesis itself
The medieval doctrine of acedia translated into modern fantastic terms
context: Tolkien's Letter 131 to Waldman summarizes the entire legendarium. The fall begins with possessive love — wanting to own and control what one has made or what one loves, instead of letting it remain free. Fëanor's love for his Silmarils, Sauron's love for order, Saruman's love for knowledge — all become possessiveness. Tolkien rejected explicit allegory but favored 'applicability' (the reader's freedom to make connections). The full Waldman letter is reprinted as the preface to the 1977 Silmarillion edition.

question: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics first appeared in a formalized statement in his March 1942 Astounding story 'Runaround.' But the concept had been gestating in earlier robot stories, especially 'Liar!' (May 1941) and the 1939 'Robbie' (which was reprinted in I, Robot in 1950). The Three Laws were not Asimov's invention alone — they were developed in conversation with which legendary editor, who later claimed (in jest, but with some truth) to have drafted them himself?
context: Campbell pushed Asimov to systematize the rules across the robot stories, and in dinner-table conversations the Three Laws emerged. Campbell pointed at the formulation in a 1947 letter and Asimov said 'You did formulate them, John.' Asimov added the Zeroth Law (a robot may not harm humanity) in Robots and Empire (1985). The Three Laws have been adopted, debated, and challenged in real robotics ethics for decades; Stanford's HAI program has discussed them as an early ethical-AI framework.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 story The Murders in the Rue Morgue introduced not only the world's first fictional detective but also the genre's bag of tools — the eccentric brilliant amateur, the slow-witted narrator-friend, the locked-room puzzle, the dramatic culminating reveal. Dupin solves the murders with a method Poe called what — a term that would eventually be borrowed for cryptography, criminology, and the cognitive sciences?
context: Poe used 'ratiocination' as a noun for systematic, reasoning analysis. He published three Dupin stories — Rue Morgue (1841), Marie Rogêt (1842), and The Purloined Letter (1844). Dupin's method blends induction from physical clues, deduction from behavior, and what we would now call profiling. Conan Doyle adopted nearly all of Poe's apparatus for Sherlock Holmes. Poe's term 'ratiocination' was the closest the 1840s came to articulating what twentieth-century cognitive science would call 'analytical reasoning.'

question: The Call of Cthulhu, published in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales, contains a specific moment that Lovecraft scholars have identified as the literary birth of cosmic horror as a self-aware genre. In Part III of the story, the Norwegian sailor Gustaf Johansen's manuscript describes his crew of the schooner Emma making landfall on the strange island that has just emerged from the South Pacific. The island's geometry is non-Euclidean — angles that should be convex appear concave to the eye. A massive door in the cliff-face swings open inward and outward simultaneously. Cthulhu emerges. Johansen's specific physical description of the door's geometry was so striking it became a literary reference point for non-Euclidean geometry in horror writing. What did Lovecraft call the geometry of R'lyeh in the story?
answer: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
choices: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
'Made of corners that opened sideways from sanity itself'
'A geometry of impossible curvature that bent the gaze of the beholder'
'Carved against the laws of Euclid by a mathematics older than men'
context: Lovecraft had been reading popular accounts of Einstein and Riemann throughout the 1920s. His 1928 phrase 'spheres and dimensions apart from ours' was a science-aware way of conveying that R'lyeh's geometry obeyed rules incompatible with our spacetime. The Emma's voyage starts in New Zealand in March 1925 and ends with Johansen alone, surviving to write the manuscript in Oslo. The story's three-part structure — the professor's papers, the New Orleans cult raid, and the Norwegian's account — gives it a documentary feel Lovecraft would refine throughout his career.

question: Tolkien wrote 'The Riddles in the Dark' chapter of The Hobbit in 1932, in its first published form. In that original 1937 version, Gollum was less monstrous — and the chapter's logic, structure, and outcome were noticeably different from what readers know today. Tolkien rewrote the chapter substantially in 1947 to make it consistent with the just-completed Lord of the Rings, in which the Ring needed to be a sinister object Gollum would never willingly give away. The most important plot change between the 1937 and 1947 versions of the chapter centered on what?
answer: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
choices: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
In 1937 the cave was located in the Misty Mountains; in 1947 Tolkien moved it to the Iron Hills
In 1937 Bilbo defeated Gollum in single combat; in 1947 Tolkien revised the contest to a true riddle exchange
In 1937 Gollum had no name; in 1947 Tolkien gave him the Sméagol backstory and the river-folk origin
context: Tolkien justified the 1947 rewrite as a textual correction — within the in-story conceit, Bilbo had originally told the Riddles chapter wrongly in the Red Book of Westmarch, then later told the true version to Frodo and Gandalf. The 1951 second edition of The Hobbit reflects this rewrite; copies of the 1937 first edition with the original benign Gollum are extremely valuable to collectors. Tolkien himself wrote in a 1959 letter that the original chapter 'gave a wholly different impression of the chief character.'

question: Robert E. Howard's Conan stories ran in Weird Tales from December 1932 until October 1936 — twenty-one stories total. The very last Conan story Howard wrote before his suicide in June 1936 was a novel-length work, not a magazine story. It was rejected by every major magazine of the era and only saw print posthumously, in serialized form, in Weird Tales over the December 1935 through April 1936 issues — the final months of Howard's life. The novel introduced the Black Stone of Set, the ancient sorcerer Thoth-Amon, and the desperate Aquilonian king Conan in the most directly political of the Conan stories. What was the novel titled?
answer: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
choices: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
The Phoenix on the Sword (the original Conan debut)
Beyond the Black River (the frontier-Pictish horror)
context: Hour of the Dragon was Howard's only full-length Conan novel. He wrote it in late 1934 and early 1935 specifically to crack the British hardcover market, which Weird Tales editor Farnsworth Wright had urged him to pursue. The novel was rejected by every house. The serialization in Weird Tales' final months of Howard's life (Dec 1935 - Apr 1936) was its first publication. Gnome Press's 1950 republication as Conan the Conqueror was the first hardback Conan. Frazetta's painting for the 1967 Lancer paperback edition is the iconic Conan-on-throne image.

question: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House in October 1939 with a single specific purpose: to keep H.P. Lovecraft's work in print after Lovecraft's 1937 death. The press's first publication, in November 1939, was a thick hardback collection of Lovecraft's best stories, edited from Lovecraft's manuscripts in Sonia Greene's possession. The print run was small. Each copy sold at a price comparable to a paperback today — but most went unsold for years; copies sat in Derleth's Sauk City basement until the late 1940s. The print run of the first edition was tiny enough that surviving copies are now among the most valuable horror books on the market. What was the original print run of Arkham House's first publication?
context: The Outsider and Others (1939) was 553 pages. Derleth and Wandrei calculated they needed about 1,268 sales to break even at the $3.50 cover price. They financed the print run from their own pockets — Derleth had small royalties from his Wisconsin regional novels, and Wandrei was a stockbroker. By the 1990s, mint first-edition copies were selling for over $5,000; in the 2010s, signed copies reached $10,000+. Arkham House remained continuously in operation under Derleth, his son April Derleth, and current ownership.

question: Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? was bought by Ridley Scott's team for a Hollywood adaptation in the late 1970s. Hampton Fancher and David Peoples wrote the screenplay. Dick was suspicious of the project — until he saw a 20-minute rough cut at Warner Bros. in October 1981 and was deeply moved. He died of stroke in Santa Ana on March 2, 1982, three months before the film's June release. The film's iconic 'Tears in Rain' monologue, spoken by Rutger Hauer as the dying replicant Roy Batty, was rewritten by Hauer himself on the night before shooting. What 1996 biographer recorded Hauer's full account of writing the speech?
answer: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
choices: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
Jerry Pournelle, in his Galaxy column
Roger Ebert, in his 1992 Great Movies
Pauline Kael, in the 1982 New Yorker
context: Sammon's Future Noir (1996, revised 2007) remains the definitive making-of book on Blade Runner. Hauer reduced what was a longer scripted speech to its iconic core: 'I've seen things you people wouldn't believe. Attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion. I watched C-beams glitter in the dark near the Tannhäuser Gate. All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain. Time to die.' The original script lines (which Hauer kept) were technical descriptions of off-world warfare; Hauer transmuted them into poetry. Ridley Scott has called it the single most moving line ever written for him.

question: The Silmarillion, published by Christopher Tolkien in 1977 four years after his father's death, is the central mythological background to all of Tolkien's Middle-earth fiction. The book's First Age narrative centers on three holy jewels — the Silmarils — wrought by the Elf-king Fëanor of the Noldor in Valinor. The Silmarils contain the light of the Two Trees of Valinor before they were destroyed. Each gem's particular quality is what makes them irreplaceable. They are stolen by the first Dark Lord (Morgoth, Sauron's master), set into his iron crown, and become the focus of three Ages of war. What specifically did Fëanor put into the Silmarils that no other gem ever made could contain?
answer: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
choices: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
The first stars Varda had kindled in the sky during the elves' awakening at Cuiviénen
A drop of the blood of the Vala Aulë, shed during the forging of the Dwarven Seven Fathers
The compressed essence of Eru Ilúvatar's first creative thought before the Music of the Ainur
context: The Two Trees of Valinor were the original source of light in Tolkien's cosmos, made by Yavanna at the beginning of the world. Telperion was silver, Laurelin gold. Morgoth (Melkor, the first Dark Lord) allied with the great spider Ungoliant to destroy them, drinking their light into her void. Fëanor's three Silmarils contained the only surviving light of the Two Trees. After Morgoth's defeat at the end of the First Age, one Silmaril rises into the heavens as the morning/evening star Eärendil; the other two are cast into the sea and the earth by Maedhros and Maglor.

question: Tolkien's friend C.S. Lewis converted from atheism to Christianity (specifically, to Anglicanism) in 1931 after a long evening walk and conversation with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson along Addison's Walk at Magdalen College, Oxford on the night of September 19, 1931. The conversation centered on Tolkien's argument that the pagan myths Lewis loved — Balder, Adonis, the death-and-resurrection patterns — were 'splintered lights' pointing toward the one true myth that had actually happened in history. Tolkien recorded this conversation in a poem Lewis cited as personally important in his religious thought. What was that 1931 Tolkien poem titled?
choices: The Lay of Aotrou and Itroun
context: Mythopoeia is a 148-line poem written for Lewis. Its key argument: man is a 'sub-creator' bearing 'the refracted Light through whom is splintered from a single White / to many hues, and endlessly combined / in living shapes that move from mind to mind.' Lewis's account of the conversation is in Surprised by Joy (1955) and in a letter to Arthur Greeves dated 18 October 1931. Lewis converted to theism in 1929 and to Christianity specifically after the Addison's Walk conversation. Mythopoeia was published posthumously in Tree and Leaf (1964) with 'On Fairy-Stories' and 'Leaf by Niggle.'

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1849 death in Baltimore on October 7 remains the most-discussed literary death in American history. He was found four days earlier — October 3 — outside Ryan's Tavern at 4th and Lombard, delirious, wearing someone else's clothes (a cheap stained suit, not the formal black he had been seen in days before), unable to explain who had clothed him or where he had been. He was taken to Washington College Hospital. Over four days of fever and delirium, he refused to drink alcohol though it was offered. He repeatedly called out one name — Reynolds — that no biographer has ever conclusively identified. He died early on October 7, aged 40. The leading modern theory, advanced by which figure in 1996, holds that Poe died of an animal-borne illness incompatible with the supposedly drunken state in which he had been found?
answer: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
choices: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
Dr. John Carlson, the medical historian who proposed encephalitis
Dr. Marie-Claude Caron, the French academic who proposed brain tumor
Dr. Peter Kennedy, the Edinburgh neurologist who proposed Lyme disease
context: Benitez presented the rabies hypothesis at a 1996 medical history conference and published it in the Maryland Medical Journal. His argument: Poe's symptoms (delirium, hydrophobia-like aversion to drink, perspiration, hallucinations) match rabies's presentation; alcoholism alone does not explain the four days of symptoms before death. Competing theories include cooping (election-day kidnapping for repeated voting), brain tumor, syphilis tertiary, and heavy-metal poisoning. The mystery of who clothed Poe, where he had been, and who 'Reynolds' was remains unsolved.

question: John W. Campbell, editing Astounding Science-Fiction from 1937 through 1971, published in the August 1938 issue a novella that became the basis for two classic Hollywood films — Howard Hawks's 1951 The Thing from Another World and John Carpenter's 1982 The Thing. Campbell wrote the novella himself under his Don A. Stuart pseudonym. The story is set at a fictional Antarctic research station. Twelve men discover a frozen alien spacecraft and the still-frozen body of its pilot, which they thaw out in the lab. The alien turns out to be a shape-shifting predator. The novella's title literally asks the sentry's challenge; what does that title phrase reveal about the survivors' climactic problem?
answer: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
choices: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is identified by being unable to give the proper sentry response in English
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is detected when it answers incorrectly in clipped Norwegian dialect
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is found out when it cannot reply with the radio operator's call sign
context: Campbell's central horror is that the alien perfectly imitates whatever it consumes, including memory and personality. By the climax, the survivors devise a blood test: each man's blood is drawn and given an electric current; the alien-blood will react to defend itself. Carpenter's 1982 film made this test the centerpiece scene. The 1951 Hawks film simplifies the shape-shifting concept; Carpenter's is the closer adaptation. Bill Lancaster wrote Carpenter's screenplay; Ennio Morricone scored the film.

question: Tolkien's Lord of the Rings was published in three volumes by George Allen & Unwin in London between July 1954 and October 1955. Tolkien had wanted a single-volume publication; the publisher split it for economic reasons (paper shortages were lingering from postwar rationing) and to share risk across three smaller print runs. Tolkien resisted the volume titles his publisher proposed; he eventually accepted them under protest. Tolkien himself would have called the three volumes by what alternative titles, drawing on his text's natural divisions?
answer: The Ring Sets Out, The Ring Goes South, and The Ring Goes East — his proposed volume titles matching the three internal Book divisions
choices: The Ring Sets Out, The Ring Goes South, and The Ring Goes East — his proposed volume titles matching the three internal Book divisions
The Shadow Grows, The Eye of the Enemy, and The Return of the King — names that match the three Sauron-encounter phases
Mordor in Sight, Mordor Approached, and Mordor Entered — names that emphasize the Frodo plot specifically
Hobbiton, Lothlórien, and Gondor — names that emphasize the principal setting of each volume's first chapter
context: Tolkien's preferred volume titles followed the six internal 'Books' the novel is divided into: Books I-II were 'The Ring Sets Out,' Books III-IV 'The Ring Goes South' (later 'The Treason of Isengard' in one variant), and Books V-VI 'The Ring Goes East' (sometimes 'The War of the Ring' / 'The Return of the King'). The published titles — Fellowship, Two Towers, Return of the King — were Rayner Unwin's. Tolkien complained in letters that 'The Two Towers' was particularly ambiguous (which two towers? he could name at least four candidate pairs). The publisher won the argument; the published titles became standard.

question: Lord Dunsany — Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron Dunsany, 1878-1957 — was the single most important literary influence on the early Lovecraft and a major influence on Tolkien. His 1905 prose-poem collection of invented mythology was Lovecraft's primary stylistic template for his Dream Cycle stories. Dunsany wrote in a deliberately archaic, scriptural prose modeled on the King James Bible. He was an Anglo-Irish Protestant, a regular at Yeats's Dublin circle, and a Boer War / WWI veteran. His 1924 fantasy novel about a king's son and an elven princess is widely considered his masterpiece. What was that 1924 novel called?
choices: The Curse of the Wise Woman
context: The King of Elfland's Daughter combines the medieval romance form with mystical fantasy, directly anticipating Tolkien's Smith of Wootton Major and parts of The Silmarillion. Lord Dunsany held the peerage at Dunsany Castle, Co. Meath, Ireland (the castle has been in his family since the 1180s — still inhabited by Dunsanys today). Dunsany was a championship-class chess player who once drew with the Cuban world champion Capablanca. He survived the burning of Dunsany Castle during the Irish War of Independence. Tolkien wrote that Dunsany's Gods of Pegana 'made me realize a writer could create a religion from nothing.'

question: Philip K. Dick experienced a series of religious-mystical events in February and March 1974 — what he called the '2-3-74 experiences' — that consumed the rest of his life and shaped his last six novels.
