Dick spent the next eight years writing an enormous private journal of philosophical speculation about what had happened to him. The journal eventually ran over 8,000 pages. A selection was published posthumously in 2011, twenty-nine years after Dick's death. What was the published selection called?
answer: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
choices: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
context: The Exegesis is over 1,000,000 words in total. The 2011 published selection (edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem) ran 944 pages, a 10% selection of the available archive. Dick's experience began with a delivery driver wearing a Christian fish-symbol necklace; from there Dick believed he was receiving 'pink light' transmissions from a Vast Active Living Intelligence System (VALIS). His diagnoses ran from schizophrenia to temporal lobe epilepsy to vitamin overdose to genuine gnostic revelation, depending on his mood. Dick died in March 1982 in Santa Ana, California, of a stroke.

question: Tolkien's Middle-earth mythology began as private writing during WWI. The earliest surviving fragments are pencil drafts in notebooks he kept while recovering from trench fever in late 1916. One of the very first stories he drafted was the tragic doomed love between an elf-maiden and a mortal man — the seed of what became the Beren and Lúthien legend. In 1917, in Roos Wood, Yorkshire, Tolkien's wife Edith danced for him among the hemlock blossoms; he immediately connected the moment to his story. What names appear on the joint Tolkien gravestone in Wolvercote Cemetery, Oxford?
choices: Galadriel and Celeborn, the immortal couple
Arwen and Aragorn, the mortal-elven pair
Eärendil and Elwing, the lovers of the Sea
context: Edith Bratt had been Tolkien's secret fiancée since his teens. After his hospitalization in late 1916 with trench fever, Edith danced for him among the hemlock blooms of Roos Wood in East Yorkshire. They married March 22, 1916 (before his deployment to France). Edith died November 29, 1971; J.R.R. died September 2, 1973. Their joint grave in Wolvercote Cemetery, North Oxford bears the names Christopher Tolkien arranged: 'Edith Mary Tolkien, Lúthien, 1889-1971' and 'John Ronald Reuel Tolkien, Beren, 1892-1973.'

question: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University, operated by Jerry Ehman, recorded a 72-second signal at the 1420 MHz hydrogen-line frequency, coming from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. The signal was 30 times louder than the background noise. Ehman saw it on the computer printout days later and wrote a single comment in the margin in red pen. The signal has never been detected again despite repeated searches. In the world of SETI and pulp-era cosmic-mystery overlap, it remains the most analyzed unexplained narrowband radio transmission in history. What did Ehman write in the margin?
context: The 'Wow! Signal' has driven 47+ years of SETI follow-up observations. The 1420 MHz frequency is significant because hydrogen — the most common element in the universe — naturally radiates at it; a civilization wanting to be heard would choose 1420 MHz. The Big Ear telescope itself was demolished in 1998 to make way for a golf course. Ehman remained skeptical the signal was extraterrestrial but never reached a confirmed natural explanation. Antonio Paris in 2017 proposed it might have been from a comet, but the comet hypothesis was challenged by follow-up observations. The signal sits alongside the Roswell incident (1947), Patterson-Gimlin (1967), DB Cooper (1971), and Mothman (1966-67) in the pulp-fiction-adjacent canon of unexplained American mysteries.

question: Hal Foster's medieval-knight comic strip launched in 1937 and ran continuously in Sunday newspapers for over 80 years. The hero is a young Norse prince from Thule who joins King Arthur's Round Table and eventually marries an Asian princess named Aleta. Foster's hand-drawn art is considered one of the finest in comics history. What's the strip called?
context: Foster drew Prince Valiant himself from February 1937 until 1971. The strip is set in 5th-century Arthurian Britain but ranges across Europe, Africa, and even North America. King Features Syndicate distributes it. Foster had previously drawn the Tarzan Sunday strip from 1931 to 1937 before launching Valiant as his own creation. Aleta of the Misty Isles becomes Val's wife in 1946.

question: Lee Falk created a costumed jungle vigilante in 1936, considered the first hero in a purple bodysuit and domino mask. The character lives in a Skull Cave deep in the African jungle and is treated as immortal by the natives — but in fact each generation passes the mantle to his son. What's the character called?
context: The Phantom debuted in newspaper strips on February 17, 1936 — predating Superman (1938) by two years, making him arguably the first costumed superhero. Lee Falk also created Mandrake the Magician (1934). The current Phantom is the 21st in line. The Skull Cave is in the fictional African country of Bangalla. Native tribes call him 'the Ghost Who Walks.'

question: Edgar Allan Poe wrote what may be the most famous detective story of the 19th century in 1844 — a story about a stolen letter the Paris police cannot find despite ransacking the suspect's apartment. Dupin solves the case by realizing the letter has been hidden in plain sight on the suspect's mantelpiece, casually inverted and re-addressed. The story has become a touchstone in literary theory after Lacan and Derrida famously debated its meaning. What's the story called?
choices: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
context: Published in The Gift annual in 1844. The 'Minister D—' steals a compromising letter from the Queen and hides it in plain sight; Dupin recovers it. Jacques Lacan's 1956 seminar on the story and Jacques Derrida's response ('Le facteur de la vérité') are landmark texts of post-structuralist literary theory. Borges, Eco, and Auster have all written homage-stories. The phrase 'hiding in plain sight' is sometimes credited to Poe.

question: Tolkien's posthumous collection The Father Christmas Letters (1976) gathers letters Tolkien wrote to his own children from 1920 to 1943, each ostensibly from Father Christmas at the North Pole. The letters include illustrations and a running cast of characters at the North Pole — a clumsy assistant, polar bears, gnomes. What's the chief North Pole goblin's name in Tolkien's letters?
choices: Snow Bear (the rival of Father Christmas)
context: Tolkien wrote the letters for his children John, Michael, Christopher, and Priscilla. Polar Bear is the clumsy disaster-prone assistant whose mishaps drive most of the letter-plots. Father Christmas himself writes in shaky red ink (Tolkien's annotation: 'I have written this with a Polar Bear paw'). Tolkien hand-illustrated each letter. Baillie Tolkien (Christopher's second wife) edited the published collection in 1976. The 1999 'centenary' expanded edition added previously unseen letters.

question: Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes — debuted in A Study in Scarlet (1887) — was widely seen as a direct descendant of Poe's Dupin. Doyle freely acknowledged Poe's influence in his autobiography Memories and Adventures (1924). But Doyle also based Holmes physically and intellectually on a specific real Edinburgh medical professor whose deductive teaching of physical-symptom diagnosis stunned the young Doyle. Doyle had been the professor's clinical clerk in 1877-78. The professor's deductive demonstrations — pinpointing a patient's profession, region, illness, and recent travels from a single glance — were the template for Holmes. Who was he?
context: Joseph Bell (1837-1911) was Royal Edinburgh Infirmary's consulting surgeon and a lecturer at Edinburgh Medical School. He took Doyle as a clinical clerk in 1877. Bell's teaching method: a patient enters the lecture room; Bell deduces occupation, hometown, recent travel, and illness from physical evidence (calluses, sunburn, accent, gait); only then takes the formal history. Doyle wrote to Bell in 1892 acknowledging him as Holmes's model. The Edinburgh detective Hercule Poirot was modeled on a different real Belgian refugee Christie knew.

question: Robert E. Howard's 'Beyond the Black River' (Weird Tales, May-June 1935) is widely considered Howard's finest single Conan story. Set on the Pictish frontier of Aquilonia, the story is essentially a Western with Picts in place of Apaches. Conan and the Aquilonian forester Balthus must defend a frontier fort from a Pictish raid led by a shaman who commands the night and the rivers. Howard told a friend in a 1935 letter that he had based the story explicitly on real American frontier history — specifically, a 1790s war in which one tribe nearly destroyed white settlement of the Ohio Valley. Which historical episode was Howard's model?
answer: The Northwest Indian War of 1785-1795, fought between the U.S. and the Western Confederacy
choices: The Northwest Indian War of 1785-1795, fought between the U.S. and the Western Confederacy
The Powhatan Wars of 1610-1646 in early colonial Virginia
Bacon's Rebellion of 1676 against William Berkeley in Virginia
The Seminole Wars of 1817-1858 in the Florida swamps
context: Howard had been reading the American historian Allan W. Eckert's pre-publication research; he was particularly fascinated by Little Turtle's 1791 victory over General St. Clair (more Americans died at St. Clair's Defeat than at Custer's Last Stand). 'Beyond the Black River' is the only Conan story without supernatural elements until the climax. Howard intended the story as a meditation on civilization's fragile margins: 'Barbarism is the natural state of mankind. Civilization is unnatural — a whim of circumstance.'

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs invented multiple lost-world franchises beyond Tarzan and John Carter. His 1918 magazine serial about a captured German U-boat captain and a stranded American who discover a primordial island in the South Pacific where evolutionary stages of life are spatially distributed (early stages in the south, modern stages in the north) inspired the 1975 Amicus film series. The island has a peculiar geographical feature — a single navigable river running through impassable cliffs. What did Burroughs call the lost island?
context: The Caspak trilogy comprises The Land That Time Forgot (1918), The People That Time Forgot (1918), and Out of Time's Abyss (1918), all originally serialized in Blue Book Magazine. Caspak's spatial-evolutionary scheme — life evolves as it migrates north — is one of pulp's most original cosmologies. The 1975 Kevin Connor film adaptation The Land That Time Forgot starred Doug McClure. Maple White Land is the setting of Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912); Skull Island is King Kong's home.

question: Tolkien's Catholic faith shaped his fiction at every level. He converted his fiancée Edith Bratt from Anglicanism to Catholicism in 1913 (she resented this for decades). He attended daily Mass for most of his adult life. He famously wrote in a 1953 letter that The Lord of the Rings was 'fundamentally religious and Catholic' — but also that he had 'cut out practically all references to anything like religion' so as not to embarrass the story with explicit allegory. Tolkien wrote a Modern English translation of which Old English Catholic devotional text — one of the very few poetic works he completed for publication?
choices: Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest known Old English poem
The Dream of the Rood, the cross-as-narrator Crucifixion poem
Christ III, the Cynewulf eschatological poem
context: Tolkien's translation of Pearl (along with Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Sir Orfeo) was published posthumously by Christopher Tolkien in 1975. Pearl is by the same anonymous 14th-century Pearl Poet who wrote Sir Gawain. The poem features a grieving father who has lost his two-year-old daughter and dreams of meeting her, now a grown maiden in heavenly bliss. The Pearl Poet's other surviving works are Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Tolkien co-edited the standard scholarly edition with E.V. Gordon, 1925) and Patience and Cleanness.

question: T.H. White's 1958 single-volume omnibus The Once and Future King combined four previously separate novels (The Sword in the Stone, 1938; The Queen of Air and Darkness, 1939, originally The Witch in the Wood; The Ill-Made Knight, 1940; The Candle in the Wind, 1958) into the most-read 20th-century Arthurian work. The novels follow Arthur from boyhood (under Merlyn's tutelage) through old age. White began work in 1936, paused during WWII, and finally combined and revised the volumes in 1958. The 1960 Broadway musical adapted from the first volume gave the franchise its now-iconic name. What was the musical called?
context: Camelot opened at Toronto's O'Keefe Centre in October 1960, then moved to Broadway. Music by Frederick Loewe, lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner. The original cast featured Richard Burton as Arthur, Julie Andrews as Guenevere, and Robert Goulet as Lancelot. The Kennedy White House famously associated itself with the show — Jackie Kennedy named the Kennedy administration 'Camelot' in a Life magazine interview a week after JFK's assassination. The 1967 film starred Richard Harris, Vanessa Redgrave, and Franco Nero.

question: Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, completed around 1469-70 and first printed by William Caxton in 1485, is the single most important medieval Arthurian text. It compiles French Vulgate and Post-Vulgate sources plus original English material into a unified narrative covering the rise of Arthur, the Grail quest, the love of Lancelot and Guenevere, and the fall of the Round Table. Malory wrote it while imprisoned in Newgate Prison. He had been convicted of which series of unusual crimes that put him in repeated trouble through the 1450s and 1460s?
answer: Theft, robbery, attempted murder, rape, and cattle-raiding
choices: Theft, robbery, attempted murder, rape, and cattle-raiding
Heresy, treason against Edward IV, and Lollard sympathies
Piracy in the English Channel and Welsh smuggling
Counterfeiting royal coin and forging episcopal documents
context: Malory's biography is reconstructed mainly from court records. He was knight of Newbold Revel in Warwickshire, served in the French campaigns under Henry V's son, then turned to local-level criminality in the 1450s. The 1469-70 Newgate imprisonment was his final and longest. He died in March 1471 and was buried at Greyfriars near Newgate. Caxton's 1485 printed edition imposed the title 'Le Morte d'Arthur' (Malory had called the work 'The Hoole Book of Kyng Arthur and of His Noble Knyghtes of the Rounde Table'). The 1934 Winchester Manuscript discovery doubled Malory scholarship.

question: Asimov's first published robot story, 'Robbie' (originally 'Strange Playfellow' in Super Science Stories, September 1940), introduced his Three Laws — though they were not formally stated until 'Runaround' (Astounding, March 1942). In 1985, four decades into his career, Asimov added a Zeroth Law that supersedes the original three. He introduced it in the novel that united his Robot, Empire, and Foundation series into a single timeline. The novel's plot turns on the robot R. Daneel Olivaw realizing the Three Laws are insufficient to protect humanity as a whole, leading him to articulate the higher principle. What novel introduced the Zeroth Law, and what does it state?
answer: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
choices: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
Foundation and Earth (1986) — 'A robot must protect the long-term flourishing of all human society'
The Robots of Dawn (1983) — 'A robot must place collective good above individual welfare'
Forward the Foundation (1993) — 'A robot may serve humanity even at the cost of an individual'
context: Robots and Empire was the 1985 bridge novel. R. Daneel (introduced in The Caves of Steel, 1954) and R. Giskard (in The Robots of Dawn, 1983) realize they must extend the First Law beyond individual humans. Giskard articulates the Zeroth Law and immediately positronic-burns out — the strain of overriding the original First Law destroys him. Daneel carries the Zeroth Law forward into the Foundation series, ultimately becoming the secret architect of Hari Seldon's psychohistory.

question: H.P. Lovecraft died March 15, 1937 in Providence's Jane Brown Memorial Hospital. He had been keeping a detailed clinical journal of his own symptoms — intestinal cancer plus Bright's disease — because the medical observation interested him. He had refused painkillers so his mind would remain clear for his observations. His final letter, written about two weeks before death, went to a young writer he had been mentoring through correspondence — a Wisconsin author who would, two years later, co-found Arkham House specifically to save Lovecraft's work from oblivion. Lovecraft's death certificate gave his net worth as approximately $25. The Wisconsin correspondent traveled to Providence in 1939 to retrieve manuscripts from Lovecraft's widow Sonia. Who was he?
context: Derleth (1909-1971) was 28 when Lovecraft died. He had been corresponding with Lovecraft since 1926 and had sold his own first story to Weird Tales at 17. Derleth's Sauk City, Wisconsin life was anchored in regional Midwestern fiction (his Sac Prairie Saga ran to dozens of novels). With Donald Wandrei (Lovecraft's other devoted New England correspondent), Derleth founded Arkham House in October 1939 specifically to publish The Outsider and Others. The press has been continuously operating ever since. Derleth's own pastiche-mythos stories drew criticism for systematizing what Lovecraft had left ambiguous.

question: Tolkien's Anglo-Saxon scholarship was profoundly serious. His 1936 British Academy lecture 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' transformed academic Beowulf studies by arguing the poem should be read as a coherent literary work, not as a quarry for historical data. Tolkien argued that the dragon Grendel and the unnamed final dragon were the heart of the poem's meaning — not mere narrative ornament. The lecture's central claim was that Anglo-Saxon literature is built on a particular tragic-heroic worldview that Tolkien named with a specific term he traced to Old English. What was that term?
answer: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
choices: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
The Anglo-Saxon doctrine of wyrd — fate as the ultimate arbiter of all human endeavor
The Heroic Code of dryht — the warband loyalty above family or kin
The Pagan-Germanic concept of doom — the certainty of cosmic destruction at Ragnarok
context: Tolkien's central argument: Norse-Germanic heroism is unique in world literature for celebrating defiance in the face of certain loss. The hero knows the world will end (Ragnarök / Doomsday); knows he himself will die; nevertheless fights on, because that is what a man does. Tolkien contrasted this with the Greek heroic code (where the hero hopes for posthumous glory) and the Christian one (where the hero hopes for resurrection). The 'Northern theory of courage' shapes Théoden's last stand, Aragorn at the Black Gate, Frodo's hopeless climb, and Sam's mantra ('There's some good in this world, Mr. Frodo, and it's worth fighting for').

question: Howard's correspondence with Lovecraft from 1930 to 1936 totals roughly 600,000 words across 200 letters, preserved largely thanks to August Derleth and the Howard Memorial Museum. The two writers debated civilization-vs-barbarism, the New England weird tradition vs. the Texas frontier tradition, race-and-nation theory, and the proper aesthetics of pulp. Their fundamental disagreement was philosophical. In a famous May 1936 letter — written just six weeks before Howard's suicide — Howard summarized his position as follows: 'I am not what could be called a civilized man. I have always preferred...' The completion of that line became one of Howard's most-quoted statements. What did he prefer?
answer: '...the barbarian to the civilized man, because the barbarian is at base a free man'

'...the Texas frontier to the New England library, however erudite or sheltered'

question: Mary Stewart's Merlin Trilogy (The Crystal Cave, 1970; The Hollow Hills, 1973; The Last Enchantment, 1979) retold the Arthurian story from Merlin's perspective. Stewart drew on the 9th-century Welsh Historia Brittonum, Geoffrey of Monmouth's 1136 History of the Kings of Britain (which invented most of the Arthurian framework Western tradition received), and the 12th-13th-century French Vulgate Cycle. Stewart's Merlin is a half-divine illegitimate child raised in 5th-century Wales after the Roman withdrawal. The trilogy's title (and the trilogy's setting) refers to a real geological feature in Wales — a coastal site historically associated with Merlin's youth. Where is the actual Crystal Cave?
answer: Bryn Myrddin near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, the legendary home of Myrddin Wyllt, the Welsh Merlin

context: Carmarthen (Welsh: Caerfyrddin = 'Fort of Myrddin') is on Wales's southwest coast. The Welsh tradition of Myrddin Wyllt (Wild Myrddin) predates Geoffrey of Monmouth by centuries — Myrddin appears in 6th-century Welsh poetry as a battle-bard who lost his mind after the Battle of Arfderydd (573 AD). Geoffrey's 1136 History conflated Myrddin with a similar figure named Ambrosius and Latinized the name as Merlinus. Stewart visited Carmarthen and Wales extensively while writing the trilogy. Her later Mary Stewart trilogy The Wicked Day (1983) follows Mordred. The combined four-book sequence is sometimes called the Arthurian Saga.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley's 1983 novel The Mists of Avalon retold the Arthurian legend from the perspective of the women — Igraine, Morgaine (Morgan le Fay), Morgause, Viviane (the Lady of the Lake), and Gwenhwyfar. Bradley framed the Arthurian conflict as a religious war between matriarchal pre-Christian goddess-worship (centered at the holy island of Avalon, increasingly fading into the mists) and the encroaching patriarchal Christianity. The novel was a massive commercial success and a major touchstone for 1980s feminist fantasy. Bradley's posthumous public reputation collapsed in the 2010s after her daughter Moira Greyland published what specific account in 2014?
answer: An autobiographical account confirming that Bradley had sexually abused her daughter and other children for decades while writing the matriarchal-feminist novels

context: Moira Greyland's account (published in The Last Closet, 2017, after Bradley's death) confirmed long-standing rumors and made explicit that Bradley had been a sexual predator. Bradley's husband Walter Breen had been convicted of child molestation in 1990. The revelations have led many readers to reassess the matriarchal religious framework of the Avalon novels — which had presented child-rearing and inter-generational female knowledge transmission as the highest moral good while the author was perpetrating its opposite. The case has become a textbook example in literature-and-ethics teaching.

question: Robert E. Howard's complete Conan canon — 21 stories Howard wrote before his June 1936 suicide — was a foundational influence on dozens of later writers. The single most influential post-Howard fantasy-writing duo took Conan as their model when launching their own bestselling series in the 1970s — a series of novels about an exiled Earthman who becomes a barbarian warlord on a primitive planet, all written in deliberate imitation of Howard's prose rhythms. The duo wrote 17 collaborative novels in the cycle from 1971 to 1991. Who were they?
answer: Andrew J. Offutt with Karl Edward Wagner

context: L. Sprague de Camp and Lin Carter were the post-Howard Conan continuators — co-editors of the 1966-1971 Lancer Conan paperbacks with Frazetta covers. De Camp wrote the 1953 Tales of Conan (the first Conan collection to add new pastiche material). Carter and de Camp also co-wrote the 1968-1977 Thongor and 1973 Kothar series. Andrew J. Offutt and Karl Edward Wagner separately edited the Year's Best Horror Stories series, but never co-wrote a barbarian series. The exiled-Earthman-on-primitive-planet motif fits John Norman's controversial Gor series, not the Conan continuation.

question: Robert Heinlein wrote Stranger in a Strange Land between 1948 and 1960. He had been thinking about the central idea since the late 1940s — a Martian-raised human raised by Martians and returned to Earth as an adult. The novel was finally published by Putnam in June 1961 after every other publisher had rejected its length and content. It became a counterculture touchstone in the 1960s; Charles Manson supposedly drew on parts of it. Heinlein's protagonist Valentine Michael Smith founds a religious movement on Earth based on Martian principles. Smith's followers learn to deeply understand things through total empathic absorption. What Martian word did Heinlein invent for this concept — a word that subsequently entered the English language?
context: 'Grok' literally means 'to drink' in the Martian language Heinlein invented for the novel — but conceptually means understanding so thoroughly that the observer becomes part of the observed. The word entered the OED in 2002. Silicon Valley engineers adopted it widely in the 1970s; you can still find it in the Jargon File. The novel won the 1962 Hugo Award. Heinlein dedicated it to Robert Cornog, Frederik Brown, and Phil Farmer. The original 220,000-word manuscript was 60,000 words longer than the 1961 published version; the full original was finally released in 1991 as Stranger in a Strange Land: The Uncut Edition.
